# Multi-Agent Topologies — a field guide

Every multi-agent system is one of a small number of shapes, or a composition of them. This is a 2D reference for those shapes: what each one is, what it buys you, and how it fails.

No framework, no dependency, nothing to install. It's a literacy document.

**Rendered version:** [`index.html`](index.html) — a styled single page, light and dark themes, no external assets.

---

## Contents

- [The primitives](#the-primitives) — single agent, pipeline, fan-out/fan-in
- [Choosing who runs it](#choosing-who-runs-it) — router, cascade, supervisor, hierarchical
- [Improving the answer](#improving-the-answer) — MoA, ensemble, debate, reflexion, blackboard
- [Decomposition vs ensemble](#decomposition-vs-ensemble) — the distinction people most often miss
- [Swarms](#swarms--a-different-family) — stigmergy, market, gossip, handoff, actor, quorum
- [At a glance](#at-a-glance) — cost and latency comparison

A note on colour used throughout: patterns optimise for **flow** (control and routing), **cost** (spend reduction), or **verification** (quality). Very few optimise more than one.

---

## The primitives

Everything later is a composition of these three.

### Single agent

One model, one context window, tools in a loop until done. The canonical form is [ReAct](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629) (Yao et al., 2022) — interleaved reasoning and tool calls.

```mermaid
graph LR
  U[task] --> A[agent]
  A -->|tool call| T[(tools)]
  T --> A
  A --> R[result]
```

**Wins:** anything that fits in one context — which is most things.
**Fails:** context exhaustion, no parallelism, no independent check on its own work.

This is the default you should have to justify moving away from, not toward.

### Pipeline

Fixed stages, each consuming the previous stage's output.

```mermaid
graph LR
  U[task] --> A[extract] --> B[transform] --> C[review] --> R[result]
```

**Wins:** known, ordered steps; each stage gets a clean context. That last part matters more than it sounds — [Lost in the Middle](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172) (Liu et al., 2023) found recall is U-shaped across a context window, with material in the middle recovered worst. Splitting a long task into stages keeps each stage's relevant material near an edge.
**Fails:** errors compound silently downstream; latency is the *sum* of all stages.

### Fan-out / fan-in

Split work across N agents at once, then merge.

```mermaid
graph LR
  U[task] --> S{split}
  S --> A1[worker 1]
  S --> A2[worker 2]
  S --> A3[worker 3]
  A1 --> M{merge}
  A2 --> M
  A3 --> M
  M --> R[result]
```

**Wins:** independent subtasks; wall-clock equals the *slowest* worker, not the sum.
**Fails:** the merge is the bottleneck. N reports still need one reader — generation is cheap, verification isn't.

---

## Choosing who runs it

Patterns that decide *which* model or agent handles a given piece of work. This is where cost lives.

### Router

A classifier inspects the task up front and sends it to one specialist.

```mermaid
graph LR
  U[task] --> G{router}
  G -->|code| A[code agent]
  G -->|research| B[research agent]
  G -->|chat| C[small model]
```

**Wins:** cheap — one decision, no retries. Good when categories are crisp.
**Fails:** a bad route is never corrected; there's no feedback path.
**See also:** RouteLLM, LiteLLM router.

### Cascade

Attempt with the cheapest model; escalate only when confidence is low.

```mermaid
graph LR
  U[task] --> H[heuristic]
  H -->|confident| R[result]
  H -->|unsure| S[small model]
  S -->|confident| R
  S -->|unsure| L[frontier model]
  L --> R
```

**Wins:** large cost reduction at near-equal quality, because most tasks stop early. [FrugalGPT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.05176) (Chen, Zaharia & Zou, 2023) reports **up to 98% cost reduction** while matching GPT-4's performance, or +4% accuracy at equal cost — though the per-benchmark spread is wide (roughly 2–3× reduction on Overruling, 5–6× on COQA, 10× on HEQA). Note that cascade is one of three strategies in that paper, alongside prompt adaptation and LLM approximation.
**Fails:** needs a *calibrated* quality signal. FrugalGPT escalates through a pre-ordered sequence of models gated by a **learned scoring function** — not by retrying the same model and hoping. Badly calibrated means you escalate everything, or nothing.

Along with the router, this is one of the few patterns here that reliably *reduces* spend against a "always call the frontier model" baseline. That baseline matters: decomposition with cheap per-subtask workers can also come out cheaper than one expensive model holding the entire context.

### Supervisor

One agent decomposes the goal, delegates, and integrates what comes back.

```mermaid
graph TD
  U[goal] --> S[supervisor]
  S --> W1[worker]
  S --> W2[worker]
  S --> W3[worker]
  W1 --> S
  W2 --> S
  W3 --> S
  S --> R[result]
```

**Wins:** handles open-ended goals; the supervisor holds intent so workers don't have to.
**Fails:** the supervisor becomes the context bottleneck and a single point of failure. In practice, traffic concentrates here far more than the diagram suggests.

### Plan-and-execute

A planner writes the full plan up front; an executor carries out each step without re-planning between them.

```mermaid
graph LR
  U[goal] --> P[planner]
  P --> S[step list]
  S --> E1[execute step 1]
  E1 --> E2[execute step 2]
  E2 --> E3[execute step 3]
  E3 --> R[result]
```

**Wins:** cheaper than a supervisor — the expensive model plans once instead of deciding on every turn. The executor can be a much smaller model.
**Fails:** the plan is made before any evidence comes in, so it can't adapt to what's discovered. Usually paired with a re-plan trigger, which starts pulling it back toward supervisor.

Distinct from both ReAct (which decides each step as it goes) and supervisor (which delegates and integrates continuously).

### Hierarchical teams

Supervisors nested in tiers, each managing a team below.

```mermaid
graph TD
  U[goal] --> T[top]
  T --> M1[manager A]
  T --> M2[manager B]
  M1 --> W1[worker]
  M1 --> W2[worker]
  M2 --> W3[worker]
  M2 --> W4[worker]
```

**Wins:** scales past what one supervisor can hold in context.
**Fails:** intent degrades at every hop. Designing the org chart *before* you have traffic is the classic error — you get an elegant hierarchy where most nodes never fire.

---

## Improving the answer

Patterns that spend *more* compute to raise quality.

### Mixture-of-Agents (MoA)

Several models answer independently. The next layer sees *all* previous answers and refines. A final aggregator synthesises. Layers can repeat.

```mermaid
graph LR
  U[prompt] --> P1[proposer A]
  U --> P2[proposer B]
  U --> P3[proposer C]
  P1 --> L2A[refiner A]
  P2 --> L2A
  P3 --> L2A
  P1 --> L2B[refiner B]
  P2 --> L2B
  P3 --> L2B
  L2A --> AG[aggregator]
  L2B --> AG
  AG --> R[answer]
```

**Key idea:** models are *collaboratively better*. An LLM shown other models' drafts produces a better answer than it would alone — even when those drafts are individually weaker than it is.

**Wins:** open-weight ensembles beating a single frontier model on quality benchmarks.
**Fails:** cost and latency multiply by layers × proposers. Rarely worth it for routine work.

**Not to be confused with MoE.** Mixture-of-*Experts* is sparsity *inside one model* — a learned gate activates a few expert sub-networks per token. Mixture-of-*Agents* routes per task across whole models. Same name shape, unrelated mechanism.

The experts are also not what the name implies. [Mixtral](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.04088) and [ST-MoE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.08906) both found **no topic or domain specialisation** — no "biology expert" emerges. But shallow *syntactic* specialisation is real and documented: punctuation, articles, and specific tokens (Python's `self`, English "Question") route consistently, and consecutive tokens share experts well above chance. The effect is strongest in encoder layers; decoder-side routing looks close to random. So: not domain specialists, but not structureless either.

**Reference implementation:** [`togethercomputer/MoA`](https://github.com/togethercomputer/MoA) ([arXiv 2406.04692](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.04692), Apache-2.0). Reported **65.1% on AlpacaEval 2.0** against GPT-4 Omni's 57.5%, using only open-source models. The quickstart is 2 layers — 4 proposers, 1 aggregator; the advanced example extends to 3+. Its `--rounds` parameter is layers − 1. Note it was last pushed in January 2025: read it as a paper artifact, don't depend on it.

### Ensemble / judge panel

Generate several candidates in parallel, then pick a winner by vote or by a judge model.

```mermaid
graph LR
  U[task] --> A1[candidate 1]
  U --> A2[candidate 2]
  U --> A3[candidate 3]
  A1 --> J{judge}
  A2 --> J
  A3 --> J
  J --> R[winner]
```

**Wins:** cuts variance; strong where there's a defensible "best".
**Fails:** possible **self-enhancement bias**. Zheng et al. found GPT-4 and Claude-v1 gave higher win rates to their own outputs (+10% and +25%), but GPT-3.5 showed none — and the authors explicitly declined to call the effect statistically established. Treat self-preference as a risk worth testing for, not a proven law. Using a different model as judge is prudent; instructing it to argue *against* the candidate is a reasonable technique, but not one that paper tested.

**Two sub-patterns that get conflated.** *Self-consistency* (Wang et al., 2022) samples the **same** model many times and takes a majority vote — the diversity comes from stochastic sampling, and it works well. A *judge panel* evaluating candidate answers is different: there, model diversity matters, because a single model's systematic biases are identical across its own samples and a vote can't detect them. Same model for self-consistency: fine. Same model for bias-checking: not fine.

### Debate

Agents argue opposing positions across rounds; a judge or convergence ends it.

```mermaid
graph LR
  U[claim] --> A[for]
  U --> B[against]
  A <--> B
  A --> J{judge}
  B --> J
  J --> R[verdict]
```

**Wins:** surfaces hidden assumptions; good on contested factual claims.
**Fails:** expensive, can converge on confident nonsense, and often doesn't beat a single good critic.

### Reflexion loop

The agent, or a critic, evaluates the attempt and feeds the critique back in.

```mermaid
graph LR
  U[task] --> A[attempt]
  A --> C{critic}
  C -->|fails| A
  C -->|passes| R[result]
```

**Wins:** substantial when there's an *objective* check — tests pass, code compiles, schema validates.
**Fails:** with no ground truth it converges on self-satisfaction. Self-critique cannot see its own blind spot; a fresh, uncontaminated critic can.

### Blackboard

Agents don't message each other — they read and write a shared store, reacting to what appears. (Originated in Hearsay-II, the CMU speech-understanding system, 1970s.)

```mermaid
graph TD
  A1[agent] <--> BB[(shared board)]
  A2[agent] <--> BB
  A3[agent] <--> BB
  BB --> R[state]
```

**Wins:** decoupled and durable — agents can die and restart without losing the work.
**Fails:** write contention, and no one owns the outcome. Needs a dispatcher that records failures honestly, or work stalls invisibly.

---

## Decomposition vs ensemble

These two draw almost identically on a whiteboard, which is why they get conflated. The difference is whether agents answer the *same* question or *different* ones.

### Decomposition — division of labour

```mermaid
graph LR
  G[goal] --> S{split}
  S -->|subtask A| A[agent]
  S -->|subtask B| B[agent]
  S -->|subtask C| C[agent]
  A --> M{merge}
  B --> M
  C --> M
  M --> R[combined report]
```

**Buys:** coverage and wall-clock speed.
**Doesn't buy:** accuracy. Nobody checks anybody; a wrong answer in slice B is merged in unchallenged.
**Merge cost** grows with N — every report needs a reader, and that's usually the real bottleneck.

### Ensemble — redundancy

```mermaid
graph LR
  Q[one question] --> A[model 1]
  Q --> B[model 2]
  Q --> C[model 3]
  A --> AG[aggregator]
  B --> AG
  C --> AG
  AG --> R[one better answer]
```

**Buys:** accuracy and lower variance. Disagreement is signal.
**Doesn't buy:** coverage. You've answered one question N times, not N questions.
**Requires** diverse models *when the goal is catching bias* — a model's systematic errors are identical across its own samples, so a same-model vote can't see them. (Sampling the same model repeatedly is still fine for *self-consistency*, where the diversity is stochastic and the goal is variance reduction, not bias detection.)

### Composing both

Agent harnesses are a programmable substrate, not a pattern. The strongest use composes both families: decompose for coverage, then ensemble each finding for accuracy.

```mermaid
graph LR
  G[goal] --> S{decompose}
  S --> D1[dimension 1]
  S --> D2[dimension 2]
  D1 --> F1[findings]
  D2 --> F2[findings]
  F1 --> V1{3 refuters}
  F2 --> V2{3 refuters}
  V1 -->|survives| K[confirmed]
  V2 -->|survives| K
  V1 -->|refuted| X[dropped]
  V2 -->|refuted| X
```

Two details that matter:

- **Verify per finding as it lands**, not after all branches finish. A barrier between phases wastes the fast branches' head start — wall-clock becomes the slowest branch *plus* the slowest verify, instead of the slowest single chain.
- **Prompt refuters to disprove**, and to default to "not proven". Give each a different lens — correctness, security, reproducibility — so their errors aren't correlated.

---

## Swarms — a different family

Often treated as a synonym for MoA. They aren't. MoA is **structured and centralised**: fixed layers, a designated aggregator, one answer out. A swarm is **decentralised**: many similar agents following local rules, no aggregator, often no global plan. Behaviour *emerges* rather than being composed. Swarms trade control for robustness.

**A caveat on this section's boundaries.** The first three below (stigmergy, market, gossip) are genuinely emergent and decentralised. The last three are not, and are included because they're the coordination substrates you'll meet in practice alongside them: *handoff* is really a router with conversational continuity — it inherits the "swarm" label from OpenAI's SDK naming rather than from any emergent property; the *actor model* is a general concurrency model that supports centralised control just as happily (Erlang/OTP supervisor trees are actors arranged in a hierarchy); and *quorum* is a decision rule you can bolt onto any topology. Taxonomies leak at the edges, and this is where this one leaks.

### Stigmergic swarm

Agents never talk to each other. They modify a shared environment, and those traces steer whoever comes next. (Named for termite behaviour: coordination through modification of the environment.)

```mermaid
graph TD
  A1[agent] -->|leaves trace| E[(environment)]
  A2[agent] -->|leaves trace| E
  A3[agent] -->|leaves trace| E
  E -->|biases| A1
  E -->|biases| A2
  E -->|biases| A3
```

**Wins:** extremely robust — agents can die, restart, or join mid-run with no coordinator to lose.
**Fails:** no one can answer "why did it do that?"; convergence isn't guaranteed or fast.

### Market / auction — Contract Net Protocol

Tasks are announced; agents bid on fitness or cost; the best bid wins the contract. Formalised as the [Contract Net Protocol](https://www.reidgsmith.com/The_Contract_Net_Protocol_Dec-1980.pdf) (Smith, 1980) — a manager announces, contractors bid, the manager awards. One of the oldest coordination protocols in the multi-agent literature, and still the right mental model.

```mermaid
graph LR
  T[task announced] --> B1[agent bids]
  T --> B2[agent bids]
  T --> B3[agent bids]
  B1 --> A{award}
  B2 --> A
  B3 --> A
  A --> W[winner executes]
```

**Wins:** allocation adapts to load and capability with no central scheduler.
**Fails:** agents must self-assess honestly, and LLMs are famously overconfident bidders.

### Gossip propagation

Each agent shares what it knows with a few neighbours; information diffuses.

```mermaid
graph LR
  A[agent] --> B[agent]
  A --> C[agent]
  B --> D[agent]
  C --> D
  C --> E[agent]
  D --> F[agent]
```

**Wins:** no single point of failure; scales to very large populations.
**Fails:** eventual consistency only — and there's no built-in mechanism to distinguish a true belief from a false one, so both spread.

### Handoff swarm

One agent is active at a time, passing the whole conversation to a peer better suited to what's now needed.

```mermaid
graph LR
  U[user] --> A[triage]
  A -->|handoff| B[billing]
  B -->|handoff| C[technical]
  C -->|handoff| A
```

**Wins:** simple, debuggable, cheap — only one agent runs at once. Very good for support-style flows.
**Fails:** no parallelism, and context degrades a little at each transfer.

### Actor model

Each agent owns private state and a mailbox. Everything happens by message; nothing is shared.

```mermaid
graph LR
  A[actor + inbox] -->|msg| B[actor + inbox]
  B -->|msg| C[actor + inbox]
  C -->|msg| A
  B -->|msg| D[actor + inbox]
```

**Wins:** no shared-state races; survives restarts if mailboxes are durable. In practice this is usually how "persistent agents" actually get built — persistence lives in the mailbox and the store, not in a process staying alive. (The model is Hewitt, 1973; the persistence framing is a modern reading of it, visible in things like Akka Persistence.)
**Fails:** message storms and deadlocks; debugging means reconstructing an interleaving.

### Quorum consensus

A result is accepted only once k of n agents independently agree.

```mermaid
graph LR
  T[claim] --> V1[agent 1]
  T --> V2[agent 2]
  T --> V3[agent 3]
  V1 --> Q{k of n?}
  V2 --> Q
  V3 --> Q
  Q -->|yes| R[accepted]
  Q -->|no| X[rejected]
```

**Wins:** tolerates individual bad outputs; the threshold is an explicit, tunable risk dial.
**Fails:** only works if failures are *independent*. Same model, same prompt, same bias — correlated errors defeat the vote entirely.

## At a glance

Relative cost is per task, against a single-agent baseline of 1×.

> **Read these as structure, not measurement.** Every cell except Cascade is *derived from the call graph* — n workers costs about n× because there are n calls — not benchmarked. Cascade cites FrugalGPT's reported range. Nothing here is a substitute for measuring your own workload.

| Pattern | Cost | Latency | Reach for it when |
|---|---|---|---|
| Single agent | 1× | baseline | Default. Justify leaving it. |
| Pipeline | ~n× | sum of stages | Steps are known and ordered. |
| Fan-out / fan-in | ~n× | slowest worker | Subtasks are genuinely independent. |
| Router | <1× | + one classify | Categories are crisp and stable. |
| Cascade | ~0.02–0.5× *(sourced)* | + escalation steps | Cost matters and most tasks are easy. |
| Supervisor | ~n+1× | rounds | Goal is open-ended, needs decomposing. |
| Hierarchical | unbounded by design | rounds × depth | Only once traffic proves you need it. |
| MoA | layers × proposers | layers | Quality is worth several× the spend. |
| Ensemble / judge | ~n+1× | slowest + judge | Variance is the problem. |
| Debate | rounds × participants | rounds | Claim is contested and checkable. |
| Reflexion | ~iterations× | serial loops | An objective test exists. |
| Blackboard | varies | async | Work must survive agent restarts. |

---

## When not to use any of this

The honest default is **one agent**. Most tasks that look like they want a topology actually want a better prompt and a longer context.

Reach for multiple agents when at least one of these is true:

- **The work genuinely doesn't fit in one context**, and splitting it doesn't destroy the coupling between parts.
- **You need an independent check.** A fresh agent can see what a degraded one can't — it's the one thing a single context structurally cannot do for itself.
- **Wall-clock matters** and the subtasks are truly independent.
- **Cost matters** and most of the work is easy enough for a cheap model.

Reasons that feel compelling and usually aren't:

- *"The steps are conceptually separate."* Conceptual separation isn't a reason to pay coordination costs.
- *"More agents means more thorough."* It means more output. Thoroughness is a property of verification, not volume.
- *"It's what a team of people would do."* Human org charts encode human constraints — attention limits, employment, politics — that don't transfer.

And the cost nobody counts up front: **coordination itself**. State passing, serialisation, partial failures, and above all the reader at the end. N agents produce N outputs, and every one still needs someone to read, reconcile and act on it. That merge is usually the real bottleneck, and it doesn't parallelise.

## Two things worth carrying away

**MoE and MoA share a name and nothing else.** MoE is sparsity inside one model; MoA is composition across models.

**Almost every pattern here trades compute for quality or for cost.** The cascade and the router are the ones that most reliably *reduce* spend — measured against a baseline of sending everything to the frontier model — and both depend on a calibrated quality signal you have to build yourself. Decomposition can also reduce spend, but only if the workers are genuinely cheaper models; otherwise it just spreads the same cost across more calls.

Composition is normal. A supervisor whose workers are cascades, writing to a blackboard, with a judge panel on the output, is four patterns and one system.

## Corrections

This guide was drafted in one pass and then fact-checked adversarially by two independent models. Four substantive errors were found and corrected before it went anywhere: a cascade cost figure that didn't match its own cited source, an overstatement of self-enhancement bias that the source paper explicitly declines to claim, an incorrect assertion that MoE experts show no interpretable specialisation, and a conflation of self-consistency with judge panels. Corrections and additional patterns are welcome — open an issue.
